label: Graph Theory
notes: Open the chapter. Graphs are the combinatorial data structure at the center of geometric deep learning. The deck follows PDF pages 65 through 77 and covers graph definitions and representations, walks and connectivity, key matrices, and the message-passing abstraction that defines graph neural networks.

label: Graphs and Representations
notes: Define a graph as a set of vertices and edges, with directed, weighted, and attributed variants. Representations include adjacency matrix, adjacency list, and edge list, each with different storage and access trade-offs. The chosen representation shapes the efficiency of learning algorithms on the graph.

label: Walks, Paths, and Connectivity
notes: Cover walks, paths, cycles, and connectivity, including connected components and shortest paths. The k-th power of the adjacency matrix counts walks of length k, linking combinatorics to linear algebra and explaining how information propagates over multiple hops in a graph network.

label: Graph Matrices
notes: Introduce the adjacency, degree, and Laplacian matrices and their spectra. These matrices connect graph theory to the spectral methods of the previous chapter. Eigenvalues reveal connectivity, bipartiteness, and clustering structure that guide both analysis and architecture design.

label: Message Passing
notes: Define the message-passing framework: each node aggregates transformed features from its neighbors and updates its own representation, repeated over layers. This permutation-equivariant scheme is the unifying abstraction of graph neural networks and ties together the algebraic and spectral foundations of the book.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter and the foundations. Graphs give a flexible combinatorial domain, walks and matrices connect structure to linear algebra and spectra, and message passing turns these foundations into learnable, symmetry-respecting architectures. The algebraic, analytic, geometric, and combinatorial threads now form one toolkit.
